title: Romania's Fragile New Government Faces Twin Crises of Deficit and Inflation
excerpt: Romania has ended nearly six months of political paralysis with the approval of Luca Niculescu's minority cabinet, but the relief may be short-lived. The new government must reduce one of the European Union's largest deficits while citizens grapple with inflation running at 7.0 percent and near-zero economic growth. The central question is whether Bucharest can restore fiscal credibility without imposing the full cost on households already stretched by rising prices.
body:
A Confidence Vote That Solves Less Than It Seems

Romania's parliament approved the Niculescu cabinet by 280 votes to 58, bringing an end to a deadlock that had left the country without a functioning government for the better part of six months. The confidence vote was welcomed by markets and European partners as a necessary first step toward restoring political order. Yet the margin of approval masks a deeper structural fragility: the cabinet holds no guaranteed parliamentary majority and will depend on shifting coalitional support to advance each piece of legislation.

The Social Democratic Party's backing has been presented by government allies as a stabilising compromise, one that prevents snap elections and gives the cabinet sufficient votes to begin work on a budget revision, the 2027 fiscal plan and energy policy. Officials argue that political paralysis had itself become an economic liability, deterring investors and complicating negotiations with the European Commission over Romania's excessive deficit procedure.

Opposition parties and trade unions are less persuaded. They argue that a confidence vote does not equal durable political authority, and that a minority government dependent on transactional support will struggle to pass the unpopular fiscal measures that genuine deficit reduction requires. Every vote on public-sector pay, pension adjustments or tax changes becomes, in effect, a fresh test of survival.

A Deficit Too Large to Ignore and an Inflation Too High to Dismiss

The numbers confronting the new cabinet are stark. The European Commission has projected Romania's fiscal deficit at 6.2 percent of GDP in 2026 and 5.8 percent in 2027, both far above the EU's 3.0 percent reference value and among the highest in the bloc. The government has set a target of returning below 3.0 percent by 2030, a timeline that implies sustained consolidation across multiple budget cycles and, almost certainly, multiple governments.

The economic backdrop makes that task harder. The Commission's spring forecast projected real GDP growth of just 0.1 percent in 2026, meaning any rapid fiscal tightening risks compressing what little demand remains in the economy. The National Bank of Romania has held its key interest rate at 6.50 percent, a signal that policymakers regard inflation as the more pressing threat and are not prepared to ease financial conditions in the near term.

Annual inflation stood at 7.0 percent in the Commission's 2026 projection, and the National Bank's own deliberations suggested the figure could exceed its earlier forecast of 6.1 percent by year-end. That combination of high inflation and near-stagnation leaves policymakers in an uncomfortable position: the tools available to fight one problem tend to worsen the other. Raising interest rates further restrains credit and investment; loosening fiscal policy risks entrenching price pressures and deepening the deficit.

Households Absorb the Pressure While Brussels Watches

For Romanian citizens, the macro debate translates into a concrete and immediate squeeze. Even if annual inflation gradually declines toward the Commission's 2027 projection of 3.7 percent, prices do not fall back to previous levels; they simply rise more slowly. Families are therefore managing the accumulated effect of several years of sharp increases in food, energy, housing and credit costs, with little immediate prospect of relief. Trade unions have warned that if deficit reduction is pursued through wage restraint, pension freezes or public-sector cuts, the burden will fall disproportionately on those least able to absorb it.

The European Union has a direct institutional interest in the outcome. Romania's repeated failure to bring its deficit within the treaty limit has already placed it under the bloc's excessive deficit procedure. Brussels wants credible consolidation, but the Commission's own forecasts acknowledge the growth constraint. Excessive austerity in a near-stagnant economy could deepen a downturn, undermine tax revenues and paradoxically make the deficit harder to close. Insufficient consolidation, by contrast, risks eroding investor confidence and straining Romania's standing within the eurozone's rules-based architecture, even as Bucharest has not yet adopted the single currency.

The Niculescu government's credibility will ultimately be measured not by the parliamentary vote that brought it into office but by what it delivers in the months ahead. A realistic budget, a transparent deficit path and an honest account of why prices may eventually stabilise while the cost of living remains high are the benchmarks that citizens, markets and European partners will use to judge whether this government represents a genuine turning point or simply a pause before the next political crisis.
